speechtext:

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REASON DR. MORGENTALER GRANTED NEW TRIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reasons upon which I acted are set out in the statement I made last Thursday, and I will be happy to supply the hon. member with a copy if he wishes or table one in the House. Briefly paraphrasing, they are a result of the decision of the court of appeal of the province of Quebec last Tuesday, which indicated that the law of necessity is a recognized defence in law, and that there was in the second trial sufficient evidence to go to a jury. On the submission of counsel for Dr. Morgentaler, I felt there was similar evidence available for the first trial and that a new trial should be ordered. Second, I felt that parliament was soon to pass-as it did yesterday-Bill C-71, which limits the right of a court of appeal on application by the Crown to either order a new trial or deny the appeal, and that the one man who had caused parliament to act in this way should receive the benefit of that provision. Those essentially were my two reasons, and they were set out in my statement of last Thursday.
In so far as the second part of the question of the hon. member is concerned, I think he is not quite correctly interpreting the law. Section 617 of the Criminal Code makes it very clear that the federal Minister of Justice has the authority and the right in special cases, upon inquiry, to order a new trial in any case which fits within the section. This is not a precedent. That is a section which has been used on a considerable number of occasions throughout the history of the criminal law.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: ALLEGED DANGER IN USE OF ARTIFICIAL FOOD COLOURING RED 2-ACTION TO PROTECT CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the concern which has developed about the artificial food colouring known as Red 2, which appears to be a health hazard and is being banned in the United States, can the minister state what steps his department is taking regarding Red 2 in order to protect the health of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DANGER IN USE OF ARTIFICIAL FOOD COLOURING RED 2-ACTION TO PROTECT CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my department has considered very seriously the U.S. government's decision on the so-called Red Dye No. 2. We are consulting the members of the European Economic Community on this matter as well as the U.S. scientific authorities. I am advised by my department that it is not deemed appropriate for the moment to take any steps in this respect, and we are not in agreement with the decision taken by the U.S. authorities in this respect.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fairweather:
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF LAW REFORM COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission in its final report on evidence. The bill is an integral reproduction of the commission's draft, and I acknowledge freely that I have used their draft in every respect but one. In that case I felt that the commission had gone too far, and I would have excluded evidence of the victim's character in sexual cases for purposes of disposition. I wanted to bring this bill before the House before the retirement of Mr. Justice Hartt, because I believe this House owes it to Mr. Justice Hartt to adopt at least one of

speechtext:
that Bill C-68, an act to amend the Medical Care Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish today to move second reading of Bill C-68. In doing so I would like to ask the House to consider first of all the recent development and accomplishments of the Canadian health care delivery system.

I think it fair to say that Canadians enjoy one of the best health care systems in the world. Federal-provincial programs have been in effect since 1958 for hospital care and since 1968 for Medical Care. These programs are based on the principles that they should be available to all residents; that they should be comprehensive; that they be publicly administered; and that the benefits be portable from one province to the other in the case of interprovincial migration and during periods of temporary absence anywhere in the world.
As a result of these programs, virtually the whole population of Canada is at present insured against the costs of necessary hospital and medical care. The federal contributions for these plans come from general revenue. Sources of provincial contributions vary from province to province. The coverage offered is total, in that there is no upper limit to the insured services which may be received as long as they are medically required.
Generally, no payment is required from the patient at the time of service. In addition to these basic medical and hospital care programs that are cost-shared by the federal and provincial governments, the provinces have added other services on an individual priority basis such as home care, dental care for children, ambulance service, prescriptions for older people and so on. The nature of these complementary services varies from one province to another.
The national programs ensure that comprehensive services are available to everyone, but they would be totally ineffective without the natural ability, dedication and excellent training of the men and women who provide these services. I am speaking of the general practitioner, the paediatrician, the obstetrician, other types of specialists, the nurses, and the many other health professionals working in the health field.
What have we accomplished as a result of these health programs? It is difficult sometimes to measure the impact of a major public program because methods for measuring the success or failure are generally not precise. Various mortality rates may be cited although improvements in these rates do not depend solely upon the adequacy of health care. There have been some dramatic improvements in certain indicators. Our maternal mortality rate dropped from 27 per 100,000 live births in 1968 to 11 in 1973, which is now one of the very lowest in the world. During the same period, our infant mortality rate dropped from 20.8 per
1,000	live births to 15.5, by-passing the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and France in ranking.
In 1973 infant mortality in Canada was 14 per cent lower than in the United States while in 1968, it was only slightly lower. We believe that these marked changes, of which we are very proud, are not unrelated to the considerable improvement in both physical and financial access to necessary care which resulted when our medical care program was added to the pre-existing hospital insurance program.
When one hears about people in some other countries where there is no universal health insurance, being faced with the prospect of losing their homes and their life savings through even one episode of serious illness, we can certainly appreciate how lucky Canadians are in comparison with others. The Canadian health insurance programs
January 28, 1976

are a very important part of our social security system. Being universal, they cover virtually all eligible residents of Canada-regardless of age, income, previous health, employment status or place of residence within Canada. Coverage is not subject to interruption during periods of lay-off, unemployment, or retirement, a feature of particular importance to the self-employed and seasonally employed residents of rural areas.
The hospital insurance program certainly solved the acute financial problems that were being experienced by many of our hospitals in the late fifties, and this contributed to a marked improvement in the quality of hospital care, thanks to more stable and rational financing. Despite predictions that the advent of medicare would provoke a mass exodus of physicians to other countries; that immigration of foreign physicians would diminish; and that medicine would cease to be attractive as a career-the number of doctors has in fact dramatically increased since 1968, the year in which the program was implemented. Indeed, this growth rate has been much higher than the growth rate of the population as a whole. This resulted from the attraction of more stable and higher incomes for physicians made possible by medicare; a rapid increase in training facilities; and, until recently, a continuing high rate of immigration.
In 1968 the doctor-population ratio was 1:769. By 1974 this ratio had become 1 doctor to 586 inhabitants. This surpassed the ratio of 1:650 that the 1964 Royal Commission on Health Services had set as a goal for 1991. In fact, at the moment, there is concern among some people- including doctors themselves-that we might be heading towards a surplus of doctors. In fact, we may have reached or surpassed that point already in some specialties. Governments themselves have become concerned about the rate of growth in the number of doctors and measures have been taken to restrict immigration. There are still several problems concerning the distribution of physicians and specialists across Canada. Still, medicare did contribute to improve the distribution of physicians by making it possible to practice in locations where there were enough people but where residents were too poor to support a physician.
Despite the high quality of health services available to most Canadians through our two major national health insurance programs, we have not yet resolved the problem of the rising costs of health services and of these programs in particular, which consume such a large part of the health care dollar.
While total health expenditures in Canada declined as a percentage of our GNP from 7.3 per cent in 1971 to 6.9 per cent in 1973, during the last fiscal year hospital costs rose by 25 per cent over the level of the preceding year. It is expected that a further increase of almost 20 per cent will occur during the current fiscal year, and medicare costs are expected to rise by about 16 per cent over the last fiscal year. Quite obviously we must take such steps as are necessary to prevent these programs becoming more expensive than we can afford, to ensure that Canadians can continue to benefit from them.
Medical Care
This pre-occupation with the escalation of health care costs is not new and goes back at least to late in 1970 when the national medicare program had not yet been implemented in all parts of the country. At that time both levels of government were concerned about the escalation of the costs of health insurance, that is, the escalation of the combined cost of hospital insurance and medicare. The federal government therefore proposed to the provinces that it explore with them alternative cost-sharing arrangements. These arrangements would be aimed at the development of lower cost alternatives to the high cost services insured under the national health insurance programs.
The essence of this proposal was to make more flexible the ground rules for federal cost-sharing in provincial health insurance plans and to cap the open-endedness of the program. Under this proposal the national standards of insured services would be retained, while making it possible for the provinces to spend federal funds on alternative lower cost services.
After nearly two and one-half years of discussion and negotiation, a federal offer on health financing was placed before the provincial governments at the federal-provincial conference of finance and health ministers in May, 1973. However, in September, 1974, the provinces formally rejected the proposal. They indicated that they would prefer arrangements that would increase federal financial participation in alternative lower cost services in return for a provincial commitment to restrain the growth of high-cost services presently supported by both levels of government. Accordingly, at the federal-provincial conference of health ministers held on January 14-15, 1975, I indicated my willingness to explore the possibility suggested by the provinces for a broader interpretation of existing federal health insurance legislation to permit additional cost-sharing. The ministers directed their officials to investigate the proposal at the official level and submit their recommendations by the fall of 1975. Subsequently, in his budget speech of June 23, 1975, the former minister of finance made it clear that the commitment of the federal government to share the costs of encouraging the development of less expensive health care services still stands.
When the former minister of finance brought down the budget on June 23, 1975, he emphasized the serious economic conditions facing our country, and announced a number of measures which the government believed were necessary to strengthen the Canadian economy. Two of these measures affect our national health insurance programs. One involved the giving of notice under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of the federal government's intention to terminate the existing agreements with effect from July 15, 1980.
While the current negotiations approved by the conference of ministers of health in January, 1975, were intented to foster improvements in the short run, there was nonetheless a general understanding amongst the ministers that the proposed broad interpretation of the federal legislation would not enable us to accommodate all of the lower cost alternatives that might be suggested by the provinces, and that another examination of the need to change the federal legislation would likely be required. In the light of this, the notice to terminate the existing agree-

January 28, 1976
Medical Care
ments under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was a logical step.
The other budgetary measure was the establishment of ceilings on the rate of growth of the federal per capital medicare contributions to the provinces. The necessary amendments to the Medical Care Act were then submitted in Bill C-68, which received first reading on July 8, 1975.
The ceilings would have permitted the per capital contributions to the provinces to grow by 13 per cent in 1976-77; 10.5 per cent in 1977-78; and 8.5 per cent in each year thereafter. The proposed ceilings would still have permitted increase in the federal contributions to the provinces of approximately 14.5 per cent in 1967-77; 12 per cent in 1977-78; and 10 per cent in each subsequent year, when allowance is made for the estimated population growth rate of 1.5 per cent per year. The purpose of these ceilings was to provide for more effective cost control. The federal government's view was that the ceilings were realistic. Not only were they in excess of the average increase in recent years, but also the rate of growth of the doctor supply, which had been the major factor causing the rise in medical care costs, was expected to decline.
The provincial governments and the Canadian and provincial medical associations nonetheless objected, some of them strongly, to the ceilings. The provincial views were highlighted at the special meeting of provincial health ministers in Victoria last summer. As a result of these reactions, I personally met with representatives from the Canadian Medical Association, and subsequently made a cross-Canada tour to meet with all the provincial health ministers. In these meetings we discussed the implications of the proposed ceilings and the need for them in the current economic context. We also reviewed the progress which had been made since January, 1975, in the negotiations on new lower cost alternatives. There was general agreement on the need to rationalize the present system. This rationalization would include the extension of insurance coverage to new lower cost services and also tighter control over the number of beds, physicians, immigration of physicians, and hence global expenditures. During these meetings the federal and provincial governments came to understand and appreciate the other's position.
It is in light of these useful consultations that I intend to propose in committee three modifications to Bill C-68. The first is to remove from the bill any reference to a specific ceilling for the years after 1977-78. Thus the bill would establish ceilings for only two years, 1976-77 and 1977-78, rather than indefinitely into the future. The bill would give the federal government authority to set ceilings for subsequent years, in accordance with an appropriate formula to be developed in the meantime, after consulting with the provincial governments. We believe this change will meet a concern, frequently expressed by the provinces and the medical profession, that it was difficult to predict accurately what might be an appropriate ceiling that far in the future.
The second change is a mechanism to ensure that any increases in the federal medicare contributions for new lower cost insured services to rationalize and improve the system would go only to those provinces providing the new services under the medical care program.

Specifically, the modification to Bill C-68 provides for a separate national per capita for each class of new insured service, if and when such classes are added. The need for this change lies in the fact that, under existing legislation, the medicare contribution to each province is dependent in part on the level of a single national per capita cost figure for all medicare services. Thus, as some provinces established new services and included the costs in the total medicare bill, the single national per capital cost would rise. The other provinces would therefore receive increases in their per capita medicare contributions. This would occur even if these other provinces had not established the new services themselves, or had established them under the Canada Assistance Plan and were thus already collecting federal payments under that plan. Separate national per capitas for each new class of insured service would solve this problem, for they would be used to calculate the federal medicare contribution only for those provinces providing the new services under the Medical Care Act. Thus the provinces providing the new insured services would receive the full federal contribution payable in respect of the services.
The third change is to provide a 36 month exemption from ceilings for new insured services from the date on which they are prescribed as an insured service under the Medical Care Act. The original bill provided for an exemption for only the first year, when costs of such services may not be very high. New low cost programs generally require at least two or three years of growth to build up sufficiently to meet all the needs which would otherwise have to be met by acute treatment facilities. It is only after this stage that their cost growth should be brought in line with the much slower rate appropriate to the more mature, existing services.
It might be suggested that Bill C-68 with the proposed amendments is no longer necessary on the basis that the anti-inflation program is now in operation. I continue to believe, however, that there are definite advantages in introducing ceilings on the allowable rate of increase of costs under the medical care program. The ceilings will provide an incentive to exercise appropriate cost control over medicare costs, for example, by encouraging prudent use by both providers and recipients of services, and by introducing lower cost alternatives to high cost services, wherever feasible.
Certainly in my meetings across Canada I received a clear indication that the provincial governments were committed to rationalizing the health system and controlling costs. They are willing to introduce low cost alternatives on a cost sharing basis and in return commit themselves to reduce the rate of escalation of high cost services. The retention of the ceiling concept will provide the provinces with an additional incentive to meet their suggested targets, for example, in the area of physician supply. It will also provide the federal government with the necessary safety valve vis-a-vis program costs if the provinces fail to meet their commitments. There is no doubt that if new insured services are to be included in the national program, both levels of government will want them to be as effective and efficient as possible.
January 28, 1976

The principles of Bill C-68, and of the amendments, that it will propose in committee are therefore consistent with the objectives of the anti-inflation program. However, it is believed that the more flexible approach taken towards the ceiling levels in the years after 1977-78 will be more acceptable to all concerned, because these ceilings can be established later in the light of more current information about the rate of inflation and other factors.

There are several ways of controlling health costs, which are currently being explored. One is to make the health care system more efficient, and this we intend to do in co-operation with the provinces. Another measure, the necessity for which emerged clearly in the working document "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", is to strengthen preventive efforts and to encourage people to assume more responsibility for maintaining and improving their own health.
Greater emphasis will be placed on reducing health hazards in the environment and on increasing health awareness among the Canadian population. Individuals, particularly those in high risk groups, will be encouraged to exercise, to smoke and drink less, to eat more wisely, and to pay more attention to accident prevention. The pay-off in improved health and well-being and the savings in health care costs could be tremendous. We have initiated a broad health awareness campaign to urge people to take more responsibility for their personal lifestyles and for their environment. Furthermore, air and water pollution, and environmental contaminants, can affect us all and the government intends to intensify efforts for their control.
Some provincial spokesmen-and indeed some hon. members opposite-have expressed alarm over the federal government's decision that costs in the health field must be contained. To help put their fears to rest, I would like to demonstrate one way whereby we could save hundreds of millions of dollars if the provincial governments, under whose responsibility this matter lies, could decide to act in a determined fashion. I am referring to the case of traffic accidents which, after heart disease, is the second most important cause of early death. In 1971, such accidents cost us 250,000 years of potential life. Human factors are blamed for 80 per cent of traffic deaths, including driving while impaired, speeding, carelessness and failure to use seat belts. This is not to mention the number of injuries on the road which totalled 223,777 in 1973 and the tremendous costs of related medical and hospital care.
The costs of traffic accidents in Canada reach well over $2 billion a year including costs of hospital care and treatment for accident victims who require over 2 million days of hospitalization. Hospitalization is estimated to cost the country at least $200 million a year and medical care costs amount to approximately another $100 million. The price tag is increased by legal expenses, public liability, property damage, loss of time from work and the costs of permanent disability.
Australia has implemented seat belt legislation over the past three years and, in the first full year of enforcement had a reduction of 25 per cent in fatal motor vehicle accidents. Similarly, France reported recently that its new compulsory seat belt legislation saved 1,200 lives in 1974.
Medical Care
The Nova Scotia Legislature in December 1974 approved such new safety measures which set an excellent precedent in Canada, although this legislation has yet to be proclaimed. It would be a great step forward in health promotion if Nova Scotia's lead in this matter were brought to a speedy and successful conclusion.
Another step in the right direction was taken when the Legislative Assembly in Ontario recently passed a provincial government bill which has made the use of seat belts mandatory since January 1 of this year. It is expected this move will mean a substantial saving in injuries, lives and health costs. A further encouraging development was the recent announcement by the Minister of Transport of Quebec that the provincial government intended to introduce legislation which would make the use of seat belts mandatory by next summer. This would be accompanied by selective reductions in speed limits on certain roads which are considered particularly dangerous. Other measures include a program of mechanical inspection of motor vehicles, tire inspection, new methods of police surveillance of roads, and review of the system of demerit points for impaired driving. I hope that the other provinces will soon follow the initiatives of Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia.
The federal and provincial governments agreed in 1974, to undertake a five-year program aimed at reducing the fatal motor vehicle accident rate by 15 per cent. The federal government, through the Ministry of Transport, and several provinces are co-operating in a three-month public education program this winter to encourage the use of seat belts as a coast to coast lifesaving habit.
Industrial safety in Canada is sadly inadequate. In 1974, 1,415 workers were killed on the job. The average for each of the past 10 years has been 1,076. One out of 20 workers had a disabling injury in 1974-a total of over 473,000 injuries. Think what these figures mean in terms of lost production, in human suffering, in social allowances, in medical and hospital care. Industrial accidents were recently estimated to cost the United States $32.4 billion annually. Canadian losses are doubtless as high in relation to our smaller population-perhaps in the neighbourhood of $3 billion a year. Can we really afford it?
Industry could do a great deal more to reduce deaths, injuries and the health costs related to industrial accidents. An interesting new program is being provided by St. John Ambulance with the most appropriate name of LIFE-Learn Industrial First Aid Effectively. It employs a multimedia course at no cost to the employee and all training is on an in-plant basis. Studies have shown that employees not trained in first-aid had an accident rate double that of their trained counterparts of the same age, sex, job and company. First-aid training in industry has another advantage: a worker can use that skill at home. A recent study shows that off-the-job injuries resulting in one or more days' absence from work, occur six times more frequently than on-the-job injuries; and fatalities are 10 times higher. This study included automobile accident. Under the LIFE program, training costs are tax deductible, a fact that many people do not realize, and I would strongly urge industry to implement first aid training programs to improve our industrial safety record.

January 28, 1976
Medical Care
Another major measure to reduce costs is to make the health care delivery system more efficient. For example, a number of lower cost alternative methods of providing health care offer the potential to produce substantial savings.
In January, 1975 as I have already mentioned, I made a special offer to the provinces in relation to sharing in lower cost alternatives but negotiations were suspended after the announcements in the June budget. I am pleased to report that the provinces are now ready to resume our negotiations and, of course, I am delighted with this development. I expect that there will be meetings of deputy ministers and of ministers of health in the near future to continue our negotiations. The federal government remains willing to extend sharing to some of the lower cost alternatives in exchange for a provincial commitment that high cost services will be controlled and de-emphasized. The lower cost alternatives being considered include less expensive types of institutional care, services provided in the home and various types of ambulatory care centres. Diversifying our methods of care can reduce the dependence on high-cost services.
The intention of the federal government is to work with the provincial governments and the health professionals to maintain and improve the system of health care so carefully built up in Canada over the past twenty years, and to ensure its continued viability by keeping the costs within the limits this country can afford. This is an objective worthy of the support of all Canadians, individuals and governments. Each one of us can contribute to the health of this country through our individual efforts to prevent illness and accidents and our prudent use of health care services. Governments must, with imagination and courage, respond to the challenge of finding ways of operating the system more efficiently.
To sum up, there is under the federal proposals, every reason why it will be possible to keep on improving the quality of the Canadian health care system. Some have stated that the proposed restraints will destroy the national health insurance programs. That, of course, is ridiculous, that is demagoguery. We are imposing realistic ceilings on the allowable rate of increase for medical care cost sharing. In addition we have given five-years notice of our intention to terminate and replace, I repeat replace, existing agreements under the hospital insurance plan. The federal government has made clear its willingness to provide more flexibility and more dollars rather than less to help improve the efficiency and effectiveness of our health care system.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize that the government is committed to a general, fundamental review of health financing arrangements. The amendments to Bill C-68 will facilitate the general review and will make it possible to proceed more rapidly with the rationalization of the system by the introduction of lower cost services, as the review progresses.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore move second reading of Bill C-68, subject to the amendments I have described.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Yewchuk (Athabasca):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has just concluded what I thought was a rather long and boring speech, so I hope the House will forgive me if I am charged with the same thing. The minister talked for a long time about many things related directly or indirectly to the health field, including references to his "new perspectives" book, health standards in this country being great compared with other countries and a number of other things. However, I am afraid in his discussion he failed to make a good case in support of the bill now before the House.
I think it is fair to say that most of us in this House who are taxpayers, or who are here representing taxpayers, will agree that government should take some kind of action to keep health costs down to a satisfactory level. But when government at the federal level is dealing with the provinces and discussing legal and binding federal-provincial agreements, any changes in those agreements should be made through the process of negotiation with the provinces. When there are these kinds of agreements, bilateral negotiations should be the order of the day. Instead we have had what amounts to a unilateral, arbitrary withdrawal from a commitment made to the provinces, which was against the will of the provinces in the first place.
When we are examining health costs, we should examine carefully where the costs have been increasing most rapidly. When we do that, we find that it certainly has not been in the area of medical care. Increasing costs, rather, have been very much on the institutional side of health costs. This bill does not come even slightly to grips with that matter.
The minister made a reference to "Perspectives on Health", a book which he brought forward in this House a year or so ago, which suggested that health costs can be reduced by changing people's life styles, by encouraging people to do fewer of the things which are destructive to their health, and I do not think anyone will argue about that. If people follow that advice, in the long-term the cost of health services will fall. Yet, paradoxically, the minister's statement runs contrary to what he has been doing these past few weeks. I am referring to the freeze of the Medical Council research budget, now frozen at last year's level. Considering that the cost of medical research went up 18 per cent this past year, freezing the budget at last year's level is the same as effectively reducing it by 18 per cent.
Figures put forward by experts in the field indicate that every dollar spent on medical research today brings a saving of $20 in health costs ten years down the road. Although the minister talks of reducing costs down the road, he is doing something which will increase costs substantially in ten years. He is reducing the medical research budget, and has never presented any logical explanation for doing so.
The present Liberal government which, unfortunately, is governing this country, has a long history of confronting various groups, whether they be provinces, professional groups, labour unions, business or private citizens. This bill represents once again a provocative confrontation with
January 28, 1976

provinces and with professional groups involved in providing medical service to Canadians. The government's present attitude in this regard is shameful. This bill represents unilateral action on the part of the federal government. It is arbitrary and has been brought forward without meaningful consultation with the provinces. Indeed, it indicates a lack of concern for the opinions of provinces in matters concerning federal-provincial agreements.
The bill proposes to limit the federal government's participation in medicare to 13 per cent next year, 10.5 per cent the following year, and 8 per cent in subsequent years. The minister said he will propose amendments in committee. Since he has not provided me with a written copy of any amendment I must rely on what I heard him say today. Today he said there will be negotiations. Perhaps that is the wrong word. There will be consultations with the provinces; but the federal government still has authority to set the ceilings.
The minister may give the appearance of backing down a little on the matter of ceilings, but I submit that he is not backing down at all. He is simply trying to take the heat off himself by saying that the government will consult with the provinces. Yet the government, as I say, still wants authority to set ceilings. Provinces will need to examine carefully the meaning of "consultation". Provinces must be careful when dealing with the federal government, as we know what it means by consultation. When the government speaks of consultation, one must not confuse such consultation with meaningful negotiation. In the past, consultation has often been a process whereby the provinces or others were simply notified of the government's decision. Therefore I am not relieved to hear what the minister has to say with regard to proposed amendments because I believe that essentially this process will not change anything in the bill. I think he will continue on his merry way, as he originally planned.
Before exposing many other inadequacies of the bill, it would be useful to review the reaction of the provinces to the bill, which was introduced shortly after the June 23, 1975, budget. I have before me copies of communications sent by the provincial health ministers. Their reactions to the minister's proposal range from bewilderment to indignation.
Clearly the provinces were unanimous in disapproving of the government's action. For example, after the budget speech was delivered in this House in June, 1975, the Ontario minister immediately called for a health ministers' conference. The conference was held in Victoria on August 18 and 19, 1975. At the conclusion of the meeting provincial opposition to this bill was virtually unanimous. The major objection expressed was that the bill represented unilateral federal government action, and that it was arbitrary. The health ministers at that time agreed to demand a meeting with the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in the hope of finding common ground on this matter as between the federal and provincial governments. They hoped the federal government might be persuaded to be more flexible.
Meeting later, the provincial premiers declared that, because of Bill C-68 and the federal government's intention to terminate the existing hospital insurance in five
Medical Care
years, the issue of cost-sharing had become their first priority in federal-provincial negotiations and discussions.
In a telegram sent to the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Manitoba minister of health said: Your government's decision to proceed with major changes on a unilateral basis is a serious disappointment to our province and, I assume, to most others ... Not only does the decision represent an apparent breach of our earlier understanding (in January) but also, and more importantly, it suggests that your government has every intention of implementing legislative changes which will cause the primary financial responsibility for the future reform of health care and for the maintenance of existing service standards to be borne by the provincial governments and their taxpayers ... It is obvious that such a decision would represent a significant threat to our national health standards- standards based on a system which the federal government itself initiated.
The Quebec minister of social affairs in his telegram to the federal minister of June 25, 1975, said:
First of all, I deplore the unilateral ceiling put on medical insurance by the federal government without warning ... One must make the distinction between an economic measure favouring the Quebec taxpayer and an economic measure destined to benefit nothing but the federal treasury-the statement by (your) government belongs to this second category.
At the Victoria conference, on August 18, 1975, the Prince Edward Island minister of health said:
The implementation of Bill C-68 would have a very serious effect on the level of health care services in P.E.I.... Our resources are severely strained to meet the rising cost with federal contributions under the present arrangement.
The Nova Scotia minister of public health said this to the Victoria conference:
I share a good deal of the concern of my colleagues from other provinces on the announcements made by the Honourable John Turner .. .
That same minister, in a letter to myself, dated July 18, said:
In summary, we regret that the government used the budget speech to advise the provinces of the limitations ...
I submit that when the minister speaks about consultation with regard to the amendments he is proposing, we can assume that he will announce either in this House or perhaps in the press what the new limits are to be after two years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yewchuk:
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Or perhaps he will do it in an election campaign.
The Ontario minister of health put the matter in these terms:
... if I have ever seen any example of unilateral decision-making without consultation with the provinces, that is it. We have been negotiating patiently for four years with the federal government to get a means of sharing health care costs that would allow the provinces to use their own discretion and to set their own priorities, instead of sharing on only those most costly services, the hospital and the physician. In the face of that, without any further consultation, they unilaterally set guidelines. They started the plan; it has got out of control. They have unilaterally limited the amount they will put into it. I don't know how we'll live within it.
The comments I have read are a fair sample of provincial thinking. I will not read all the communications in front of me, because I know others want time to speak. I also have

Medical Care
responses from the medical people affected by this measure, particularly the Canadian Medical Association.
Before I go into that, let me just touch a little on the idea that this move by the federal government is in some way going to encourage the provinces to take greater care to reduce health costs. That concept or idea put forward by the minister is nothing less than ridiculous. The fact is that the provinces are now carrying half the cost load of medicare costs. Indeed, if these costs, rising as they are, are a great motivation to the federal government to try to keep them down, I cannot see how the minister can be justified in saying that there is no motivation for the provinces to keep the costs down. The motivation is the same. The provinces must get the money from the taxpayer and foot the bill as well.
We cannot accept as legitimate the minister's claim that this kind of cap, as he called it, will provide greater motivation to the provinces. I feel they are already sufficiently motivated in view of the fact they are now paying half the cost.
The Canadian Medical Association dealt even more harshly with this bill. I suppose that is because they are very directly affected by the outcome of it. On July 10, 1975, the Canadian Medical Association declared, and I quote:
The budget controls will produce definite health hazards for Canada's health care delivery system. The government of Canada's budget controls will have the effect of restricting the availability of health care. .. in effect, rationing needed medical care, unless additional funds are provided by the provinces or the public. This action could endanger the quality of medical services available to Canadians.
The Canadian Medical Association also pointed out the arbitrariness of the percentages in this bill. The minister says that the percentages which were set are higher than the increases have been in the past few years. Perhaps this is true. However, I think it is worth pointing out at this time that over the past few years the medical associations were asked to exercise voluntary restraint in the interest of keeping down these costs. They have indeed been doing that.
The increases per capita of medical care costs in Canada from 1971 to 1972 averaged 6.9 per cent. That was the increase in medical costs, 6.9 per cent. At the same time the average increase per capita of the gross national product at market price was 12.8 per cent. Furthermore, the consumer price index for the same period rose at 7.9 per cent annually, and the average weekly wages and salaries in the industrial sector rose in the area of 8.5 per cent annually. This clearly shows that the increases in the per capita medicare costs have been lower than in any of the other areas I have mentioned.
I think we can fairly say that reasonable restraint has been practised by the medical profession in this area. Since no one else has been showing significant restraint, perhaps they feel the time has come that they should do some catching up. However, this is where the minister takes out his sledgehammer and uses it on the heads of the medical profession in order to prevent any notion of catching up which they feel justified about doing. The Research Director of the Canadian Medical Association, Dr. J. Brandejs,

on August 15, 1975, pointed out that while the budgetary ceilings may be realistic, they are arbitrary. Grounds existed, he said, for concern centring on both the immutability of the guidelines and the low social value they seem to put on Canadian physicians.
From the point of view of regional interests, they voice great concern over their inability to improve local standards of health care. They maintain that the ceilings will forestall future developments which certain provinces have been planning at this time, particularly in areas where low economic conditions exist.
When this measure was first introduced in the budget last June, the national press was not very quick to appreciate the significance of this aspect of it. They concentrated more on the gasoline tax and the over-all inadequacy of that document. But as a result of the health ministers' conference in Victoria the media began to realize just how serious an impact this legislation will have on co-operative federalism and the health care delivery system. As an example of the kind of statements made by editors on this subject I quote from the August 13, 1975, edition of The Commonwealth:
The health ministers' conference must expose the spending ceilings for the Alice-in-Wonderland unreality they represent. How does the number 13 per cent relate to economic and health conditions for the year 1976-77, for example? Who knows? Who can tell? The minister knows, but the minister is not talking.
This again points out the arbitrariness of these programs. The August 19, 1975, edition of the London Free Press contained the following, and I quote:
Unilateral actions like this are damaging to federalism and should be avoided ... Provincial governments are justifiably annoyed that they were not consulted prior to Mr. Turner's decision.
One might have added this was particularly the case because it was the federal government which had imposed this program on the provinces in the first place. That is the saddest part of all. This program was shoved down the throats of the provinces in spite of their screams of agony and despair. They did not want it, yet it was done. The federal government is now taking the first step in opting out of this program. I am sure this is only the first step. It will not stop with this bill. If the government does intend to stop, I would like it to say so in this House.
What are the implications of Bill C-68? I have already touched on a lot of them. Historically, as the leader of my party pointed out, Bill C-68 is just one more case of the Liberal government going before the provinces, making a deal, and then a few weeks later or a few months later taking some action unilaterally which amounts to a doublecross.
At the federal-provincial conference of July 1965 the then Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, announced a federal government resolution to provide financial support for provincially administered medicare plans. He asserted his government's intention to share 50 per cent of the cost of medical services if the provinces were able to meet his four basic principles of eligibility: comprehensive, universality, public administration, and portability.
It was not until the fiscal year 1970 that all the provinces were brought under the medical care umbrella. In the meantime a great deal of pressure was brought to bear against the federal proposal by provincial governments
January 28, 1976

and medical and professional associations. While the then minister of national health and welfare, currently the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), confidently estimated that the net cost of the scheme to the two levels of government would be $80 million, Ontario Treasurer Charles S. Macnaughton, speaking to the federal-provincial meeting of finance ministers in November, 1968, said,-it turned out to be a prophecy-and I quote:
What guarantee have we that in a few years from now, the federal government will not dump the full responsibility for this program on the provinces, and close off or limit its contributions after it has obliged the provinces to embark on its slippery slope?
That has proven to be exactly what is happening. I hope that if the minister has any conscience at all he feels very guilty about this state of affairs created by his party.
In those early years of the medicare concept, opposition to the federal government's proposal came from two camps and centred on two quite different principles. The provinces contended that the Medical Care Act represented federal encroachment upon an area of exclusively provincial jurisdiction; that provincial priorities were being distorted by the availability of federal dollars; that the program was untimely and uncalled for, given existing health care systems and other considerations, and that under the scheme the provinces had very little control over administrative costs, procedures, or priorities. On the other hand, the Canadian Medical Association strenuously questioned the principle of government interference with a professional body. As it turned out, both groups knew what they were talking about.
In the mid-sixties, no fewer than seven task force committees were established to study the escalating cost of health care. Appearing on the second page of their summary report is the flat statement that there were many examples of cases where economies could be achieved without in any way diminishing the quality of health care. The report itemized three pages of examples which it characterized as "just a few". It concluded with the noteworthy sum of 337 recommendations. When this report was published, a federal-provincial committee was established to scrutinize the financial operation of the Canadian health care system. This committee was entrusted with an ongoing consultative role in an attempt to revamp the financial end of the system.
More recently still, the Department of National Health and Welfare published a document entitled "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians". In this document the minister and his staff introduce a new typology to cover the health field concept: human biology, environment, life style, and health care. They described this new approach as "a unified whole which permits everyone to see the importance of all factors".
My purpose in making this brief rundown of studies and statements on health care reform is to contrast them explicitly with the content and, what is more, the intent of Bill C-68. The government had more than 300 recommendations at its disposal yet it chose to ignore all of them, opting instead, for budgetary ceilings. Mr. Speaker, the real reason for the introduction of the "health field concept" by the Department of National Health and Welfare was to advance the premise that improvements in life style
Medical Care
and environment are as conducive to good health as is medicine. Yet the government has not applied this powerful notion even marginally to the question in hand.
The third major finding of the 1969 task force report acknowledged that effective and efficient health care delivery demands co-ordinated government planning. Yet the government now unilaterally imposes budgetary ceilings thereby threatening the continued vitality of the federal-provincial consultative process. In short, however much as we might criticize the content of Bill C-68, the most distasteful part of the whole business is the fact that legislation of this sort was introduced at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Consider also the arbitrariness of this bill. If it is passed the ceilings specified within its clauses will become statutory. Although one of the basic principles of responsible government is that parliament cannot bind its successors, political realists take it for granted that reversal of procedures previously undertaken is a long and arduous process. Since health care ceilings will for all practical purposes be unalterable, the question must be raised: what if they are simply too low? What if the desired standards of health care just cannot be maintained within the restrictions of the bill? The figures seem to have been pulled out of a hat; they are unaccompanied by any explanation as to how they were derived.
In other words, by putting these ceilings into the bill the government will ensure that, as long as inflation continues and medical costs continue to increase at an accelerated rate, the taxpayer will inevitably suffer either in terms of increased provincial taxes or in terms of reduced health services. In brief, the ceilings are wrong because (1) there is no immediate reason to believe they are appropriate, and (2) there is no flexibility to them despite the lengthy time span in which it is contemplated they will be enforced.
Another way of expressing this difficulty is to say that the gross federal expenditures on health care for all ensuring years in an inflationary era will depend solely on growth expenditures for 1975-76. That is, since ceilings are calculated as a percentage increase in expenditures from year to year, and since the percentage increase for any given year will be dependent on the absolute expenditure of the previous year, gross expenditures for 1975-76 become all important. And since expenditures for 1975-76 are a quantity which is still not completely known, the government can as yet have no idea what impact the budgetary ceilings will have in the long run.
However, extrapolating from national medical care expenditures in 1974-75,-expenditures which amounted to $1.37 billion-we can calculate the consequences if outlays should increase marginally, as projected, or markedly. We know that if final medical care expenditures in 1975 were to increase by a marginal 3 per cent to $1.41 billion they could rise to no more than $2.54 billion by 1980. Were expenditures to increase by a quite conceivable 15 per cent in 1975-the minister said 16 per cent-they could, on the other hand, stand at $2.86 billion by 1980, a third of a billion dollars more. It is worth nothing that the increase projected by the government, at 6.5 per cent, can itself be described as a marginal one.

January 28, 1976
Medical Care
Confronted with a situation such that a difference in expenditures of $.17 billion in 1975 could result in a difference of $.32 billion in capital outlay in 1980, the provinces would be foolish not to attempt to hand the federal government the largest medical care bill possible in the base year. Instead of lowering health care costs, Bill C-68 will actually raise them.
To sum up, it is quite impossible to forecast accurately what is going to happen to medical care in Canada in the light of the changes suggested in Bill C-68. Because the long term shape of health care services in Canada is dependent on so many usually conflicting variables, and facts are not easily quantified, it is nothing but frivolous to seek to predict the future of this field in blind confidence. Nevertheless that is exactly what the government has done in introducing Bill C-68.
Spokesmen for the government will no doubt argue that the imposition of ceilings on federal contributions will not impose undue strain on provincial coffers and will not result in any significant reduction in health services. Let us suppose for the sake of argument that all goes according to plan-that the guidelines encourage provincial restraint and constitute a positive input into the plan's budget forecasting. Because doctors' fees make up a large part of medicare's budget this state of affairs will come about only if the cost of doctors' services does not rise above the budgetary ceilings. But if the cost of those services does rise above the ceilings the government is in fact imposing wage controls on a single identifiable professional group. I know this has altered somewhat with the anti-inflation program, which has placed some limits on all professional incomes, but when the anti-inflation program was introduced the bill was to be in effect for three years. That is a temporary measure, but Bill C-68 is not temporary, it is permanent.

It still remains to be seen whether indeed the anti-inflation program will be temporary; if we listen to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) which he made a while ago we might conclude that the program will not be temporary at all. The fact is that Bill C-68 places permanent wage controls on the incomes of professional groups that provide medical services to the people of Canada, which seems to me to be rather discriminatory against one specific professional group.
Few would disagree with the view that the federal government, because it is responsible for the over-all scrutiny of the economy, must have the power to control its own budget. To a certain extent it is true that the open-endedness of the financial aspect of medicare is such that the central government cannot monitor its expenditures on a year to year basis. However, the statistics of the matter offer some rather valuable insights into the urgency of these arguments.
The former finance minister, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), maintained that health care costs have risen almost 20 per cent over the last fiscal year. The hon. member was correct in his figure of 20 per cent no doubt, but what he neglected to mention was that the great bulk of this increase was the direct result of escalating expenditures, not in medical but in hospital

care. In fact the figures demonstrate quite clearly that in the last two years for which statistics are complete, 1972-73 and 1973-74, the increase in medical costs has been only 9.2 and 7.2 per cent respectively. In 1971 the figure was 6.9 per cent per year, as I have already mentioned. Furthermore, the figures show very plainly that since the time when the medical care system matured, the costs to the federal government have not been increasing at a rate greater than national income.
So why did the central government arbitrarily decide to establish spending ceilings on a program which has not demonstrated the run-away cost increases of other federally sponsored projects? The answer probably lies in the fact that between 70 and 80 per cent of the total cost of medical care consists of salaries and wages. During a period of inflation and rapid wage escalation such as we have been experiencing, a 20 per cent increase in wages would result in a 14 to 16 per cent increase in total budgetary outlay. By imposing these ceilings the federal government hoped to ensure that it would not have to pay medical costs which are a direct result of its inability to control inflation.
More disturbing than federal deviousness are the prospects for increased taxes and decreased services. Granted that expenditures may appear to be under control, there are signs that a rapid upturn in the capital outlay required to maintain health standards is imminent. For example, Ontario physicians received and increase of only 4 per cent in their fee schedule in 1974 and recently were asking for 20 per cent in 1975. In addition, many provinces maintain that they need a catching up period in order to raise their regional standards to national levels. Either event occurring could cause a marked increase in medical care expenditures, and under the stimulus of Bill C-68 both are likely to occur at least in 1975-76 before the limits go into effect.
So while the federal government has introduced these ceilings avowedly in order to encourage economies in medical care, the bill does not even ensure economies. Nothing in the act actually stops the provinces from improving their health care services, and nothing actually stops physicians, after the expiry of the Anti-Inflation Act, from demanding heftier salaries. All the bill does ensure is that, if either of these events should occur, it is the provinces which will have to pick up the additional costs, either in the form of increased premium rates or in depleted provincial revenues, perhaps at the sacrifice of other provincial programs. Thus the analogy to be drawn is not one of the government slapping the hand that reaches into the taxpayer's pocket, but another, that if there is a need to pay for increased medical costs it is the provinces or the doctors who must do the reaching.
Should costs rise above and beyond the cost-sharing limitations, any one of the following three situations may develop: first, provincial revenues will be drained and other programs or priorities will have to be deflected in order to meet the increased costs; second, where applicable, as in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and the Yukon, premiums will have to be increased in order to offset greater provincial medical expenditures; or third, if the provinces cannot meet the budgetary restraints, medical services will have to be reduced.
In other words, if medical costs increase at a greater rate than that allowed by the 1975 budgetary ceilings, then the
January 28, 1976

provinces will be forced to seek those very solutions that the current Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), the then minister of health and welfare, foresaw as undesirable in his introduction to the task force report of 1969.
Equally bad are the implications for co-operative federalism. In Canada there is no constitutional mechanism or provision for the practice of cost sharing. Likewise, the federal government has no constitutional grounds for entering the health field. Both are the result of convention and the ongoing evolution of Canadian federalism. The practice of cost sharing has ensured the maintenance of national standards, while the very principle of co-operative federalism is undoubtedly one of the most distinguishing features of our nation. But the government's five year notice of its withdrawal from the present hospital insurance plan and the imposition of ceilings on contributions to medical insurance threaten both of these principles and practices.
Although it is impossible to gauge precisely the impact of Bill C-68 on our system of federalism, indications of the drift of events are already evident. The unilateral nature of this measure has outraged the provinces. Their immediate reaction was to call for the instant cessation of all cost sharing consultation with the federal government.
If the government's ploy in introducing this legislation was to "bring the provinces back to the bargaining table", as those same provinces have since suggested was the case, it is now clear that this ploy was completely misconceived. Ontario has demanded a 17 point tax transfer from the federal government in exchange for opting out of medicare. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, flatly rejected this offer, but should Ontario continue to press and eventually succeed in opting out, it would mean that the principle and practice of a national system of prepaid medical insurance would be completely thwarted. Furthermore, such an event occurring could set a disastrous precedent in the field of federal equalization.
Finally, if increased costs do occur it would be the have-not provinces which would be the first to be obliged to reduce their medical care services. In areas where the physician-to-population ratio is already low, this reduction would coincide with a marked downturn in the level of health care and would exacerbate regional disparities which we all want to try to correct.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, if the minister has been listening to what I have been saying-

One might ask why we are opposed. I am not going to repeat a lot of the points that have been so ably made by the Conservative spokesman but I do intend to repeat several, and add a couple of others. First let me point out one thing that I think distinguishes us from the Conservative party. Right from the outset of the government's anti-inflation program members of the NDP have said there are certain aspects of government spending that ought not to be cut. We have said it is irresponsible politics in Canada to suggest that across the board cuts in government spending are desirable.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said on various occasions in the House of Commons, civilization costs money. One essential aspect of civilization in Canada in 1975 surely is the provision of fully adequate medical and hospital services for Canadians in whatever part of the country they may live. Therefore, we reject this kind of categorical and arbitrary imposition of ceilings on medicare spending-14.5 per cent in the period 1976-77 and 12 per cent in 1977-78. We resent it because although it is not certain it will occur there is at
January 28, 1976

least a very real possibility that necessary medical spending in those years will exceed those limits.
The New Democratic Party for one says that if it costs money to provide needed medical services we should spend the money and cut back in other less essential areas. That is an overriding concern and an overriding commitment of the New Democratic Party. We believe this country must allocate whatever funds are necessary to achieve and maintain fully adequate health services from one coast to the other.
Second, we believe that medical services, as with services in certain other essential areas, should be provided on a federal-provincial cost-sharing basis. We believe that, because to us it is essential with such programs to ensure that the poorest parts of Canada have health services just as good and at just as high a level as the richest parts of Canada. That is the reason why the federal cost-sharing approach to medical services is absolutely essential.
Beyond these basic points, what else should be said at this time? I shall not do what the minister himself did, which was simply to rehash a speech made a year ago. I wish to deal with two, three or four essential aspects of the cost of medical services and point out for the House, and indirectly for the people of the country, that we believe an approach to spending in medical services will involve some short-run increases in expenditures which, in the long run, will provide a healthier people but also in the long run a reduction in real cost to the economy.
We will suggest some rearrangement of medical spending that could provide real benefits in terms of financial requirements at both the federal and provincial levels. First of all, it is our view that it makes sense to increase medical spending at all levels in Canada in the preventive medical field.
For us it makes neither human nor economic sense to let a man work in conditions where he is confronted, for example, with asbestos fibres which he inhales, and as a result of this contracts cancer which means that then he must go through the cruel and certainly painful and costly surgical operation which results. In such a case at that stage in the man's life we try to deal with cancer when, as an alternative, as a country, we could have been spending more money to establish community clinics in parts of our country where such work is undertaken. In this way we could have developed cures that would be less costly and more humane. We should of course eventually remove the pollution from the air which is the very cause of this kind of cancer.
I repeat that to deal with that kind of a situation now, an increase in expenditures would be involved. We say that, but we think it is a necessary increase in expenditures the long run benefits of which would result in lower medical care costs over-all because it would eliminate costly surgery down the road and would of course produce a healthier working population.
There is, for example, in the minister's own province very imaginative and constructive use of community clinics. I had drawn to my attention not long ago a good example of the result of the opening of community clinics in the minister's province in the town of St. Gabriel de

Brandon, southeast of Montreal. A community clinic was set up in this area.
Children who had been swimming in that community had been repeatedly going to doctors because of a kind of skin infection. They had been treated over and over again every three months or so. This had been going on in many sequences of three-month periods. Because this clinic had been set up with authority to carry on investigative work in the medical field it was discovered that because of the condition of the water supply the children had become infected.
Because the clinic had authority to take corrective action the company responsible was obligated to stop polluting the water. In this way the recurrence of the infection was stopped and further costs for medical services were eliminated. The point is a rather obvious but important one. Because of the existence of a community clinic in the town of St. Gabriel de Brandon the long-run cost for medical services was actually reduced because it was possible to get at the source of the medical problem and head it off before it recurred. Surely this is imaginative and positive spending. I repeat that it involves some increases now for real financial and human gains down the road.
Another suggestion we make is that we can get away from spending so much money on general hospitals. There could be a curtailment of the large expenditures we now have in respect of general hospitals which, according to the latest figures I have, involve an expenditure of about $200 a day per bed. The cost probably has increased somewhat since the figures I have were released.
Alternative facilities which would be fully adequate for most of the present hospitalization requirements could be built. These could be operated at a cost of somewhere between $42 and $52 per bed per day. The point once again is that if we were to achieve this it would not mean an over-all cut-back in spending for medical purposes, but in fact would mean an increase for the purpose of building these alternative facilities. The net result, however, not this year or next year but a few years down the road, would be a substantial reduction in the over-all cost of hospitalization.
Once again the obvious point to me, although it apparently is not obvious to the government or necessarily to the people of Canada, is that a cut-back in expenditures now does not mean that there will be necessarily a long-range saving in economic terms to the community. It is just the opposite; if you do not spend on what is needed now, with careful selection of increased spending in certain areas such as alternative hospital facilities, substantial long range savings can be achieved.
Another area of spending which will involve real savings down the road in terms of economic cost and in terms of human lives is in the medical research field. The hon. member for Athabasca very ably documented the case for increasing spending on medical research, not cutting it back as the government is shamelessly doing at this time.
Another illustration of real savings is in the paramedical field. Instead of relying so heavily on the use of general practitioners, a lot of work should be done in all provinces, including those with NDP governments, on extending the

By moving decisively into pharmacare, into controlling the drug industry in Canada, either by setting up a competitive national company to produce the necessary drugs or by some other indirect means of controlling the prices of drugs, the government could take decisive steps which would result in long range savings in the drug area.
Finally, on the whole general question of savings in medicare costs I want to emphasize the point that has already been made, that by putting arbitrary ceilings on the federal government's contributions, especially for the next two years, no saving can really be achieved in the economy of Canada in terms of medicare costs. All that will be saved is in the federal share of the total cost to the public. The costs will be paid but they will be paid for by the provinces, fully half of which are not in a good position to pay them. That is not a sensible approach to cost saving that the minister is taking.
If the minister really wanted to achieve savings, he should have fulfilled his obligation and worked out with the provinces, on a mutually agreeable basis, definite approaches to very specific programs that could lead to short run and long range cuts in costs. I repeat that the best place where the minister could go to find out what should be done in terms of specifics would be the provinces themselves. As he knows, the Science Council of Canada has pointed out that the province of Saskatchewan, for example, has the best record in the country of controlling costs for medicare services, and not only Saskatchewan but other provinces are just as concerned as the federal government about saving money.
I would remind the minister that this is a cost sharing program. The federal government has no more profound an interest in saving in terms of medicare expenditures than do the provinces, but the provinces which are directly involved in providing the service also know where cuts should be made in order to save.
I remind the minister of his own commitment. If he is really interested in cutting back unnecessary spending, and if he would like to find out where new expenditures could be made that will lead to long range savings in medicare costs, he can go to no better a source in this country than the provincial ministers of health.
I want to say why we as a party are so concerned about this approach. It is because the inevitable result of the passage of this bill, assuming that the costs go beyond the ceilings permitted in the legislation for the federal government to pay its share, will be that the poorer parts of our country will certainly suffer in terms of medicare expenditures. They will suffer in a number of ways; either abhorrent deterrent fees will be increased, or a cut back in medical services will be introduced, or property taxes will be increased, or sales taxes will be increased in those
(Mr. Broadbent.]
provinces to make up for the money that the federal government should be paying for those programs.
We are so deeply opposed to what the government is doing because one of the few areas of real concern to the people of Canada to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated he might be committed in 1968 was regional inequality, to dealing with it, hopefully reducing it and ultimately removing it, but the inevitable result of this program is to increase inequalities between regions in Canada. We say that health service is the wrong field to do that.
A Canadian should be able to take health services for granted. Whether he lives in Vancouver, in a wealthy province such as B.C., or in St. John's in a poor province, he should feel fully confident as a Canadian that he will have equally available to him the best medical services in this country. What this bill does-I do not care what the minister says-is to make that possibility more remote. What it will almost certainly mean is that the poorer provinces will do two things: they will have to cut back on the services that are necessary, and simultaneously they will have to increase taxes paid by their citizens.
We think that that kind of action is totally abhorrent at this point in Canadian history both because health care is an area of service where we should have a uniformly high standard right across Canada and because it increases the general sense and feeling of inequality in our country at a time when a feeling of national unity across our land is so essential to the whole nation.
If there is any way in which we will get a profound sense of unity it will be because of the subjective feelings of Canadians in all parts of the land that there really is equality in terms of their life expectations. Our party thinks on this issue that the Liberal government is clearly moving in the wrong direction and that instead of increasing the sense of equality and the sense of well-being, founded in part on the notion of universal health standards, it is taking us a step backward.

It deals with the limitation of costs for 1976-77 and for 1977-78. I thought that it was only an anti-inflation bill to limit the cost of all health services. But, after its presentation by the minister, I realized that this bill that seemed small had many surprises in store. After the committee stage the subject matter will probably be much more heavy.
Of course, the minister started by giving glory to his party and mentioned all the good things the Liberal party did in the field of social services. But he had to go back to 1958 to realize that the federal-provincial hospitalization plan dated from that time. It is in 1958 that these federal-provincial agreements were made concerning hospitalization services, while we obtained, I think, partial medical care only in 1968. A federal-provincial agreement was then
January 28, 1976

planned concerning the hospitalization program. Medical care was supposed to be included in that project, but we had to wait 10 years before it was granted to taxpayers.
According to the minister, all hospitalization costs are paid. I agree with him on that point. But at what price? I think that we shall have to study the matter carefully at the committee stage and get some bills from the provinces to know what is the cost of hospitalization in each of them. In the province of Quebec, as I come from that province, a hospital bed costs $90 a day, which, I think is an astronomical figure considering the services given. One may praise our services and when the minister said earlier that we had the best hospital care plan in the world, I think he forgot on purpose to add that our services were not the best in the world.
In my opinion, the present weakness of our hospital care system is that services offered are not consistent with the cost assumed by taxpayers. No matter how much we criticize the services provided in the past, today's services can in no way be compared to those offered 25 years ago, Madam Speaker. We have the worst hospital services ever provided as far as admission is concerned. Nowadays, before being admitted to hospital, you must wait a couple of months. However, we are told that we offer wonderful services to everybody.
