The Minister said he intended to keep increases down to 10, 12 and 13 per cent during 1976-77. I hope he does reach that goal but I am afraid he will limit only his payments to the provinces. Maybe those payments will be kept down, but the federal government after collecting all the taxes, as it is doing now, will return whatever it feels like. The decision will be the governement's, be it maybe 8, 10 or 12 per cent.
Let us not forget that the provinces are responsible for hospital services and will still have to pay the difference. If the tax rate is 20 or 25 per cent, the federal government will have no part in it, but the provinces will have to make up the difference in order to provide adequate service. As always, the government will pocket the money and the provinces will have to foot the bill.
The meaning of the 12 per cent limit must be fully grasped. In committee as in this House, we are happy to hear of spending limitations, but the understanding with the provinces must be honoured. If that understanding cannot be honoured, then we must do what is needed, we must give the provinces back their taxing rights in order that they administer medicare themselves. This way they will not have to keep on begging the federal government to pay this or that, an expensive process because with duplication of departments we pay double costs. We have to pay double price for the administration. If that is the majority's will, let us honour the agreements. And above all, there must be agreement between the parties involved. Because it is getting to be a one-way proposition. The federal government submits proposals to the provinces, but before they can be discussed with the provinces they introduce legislation. And so with majority government rule the provinces are faced with the choice of either accepting or having nothing. That is the kind of consultation we get from this government.
I submit the provinces are responsible for the citizen's health. They should tell the federal government what to do, instead of the latter imposing its will upon them. The minister boasts of our health care. He says it is better than the American and the British systems. He refers to decreasing infant mortality rate, that has been at the 1.5 per cent level these last years. But he forgets to mention that the birth rate also is now down to 1.4 per cent. In Canada, the figure is 14 per 1,000, and in French Canada, 12 per 1,000 of population. It seems that we are always the winners in one way or the other. With 12 per 1,000, there cannot be more babies who die than are born. We cannot boast too much about it and it is better not to mention it at all, especially to those of us who come from the province of Quebec, because we are a little ashamed of it. In the province of Quebec, we will soon be replaced by the Chinese and the Japanese. Anyway, with such a birth rate, we cannot do more here, I quite agree with my friends on the other side, we are doing our best.
The minister mentioned the increased number of physicians. In the last few years, the number of doctors has increased but I want to point out to the minister that this increase was not due to the number of students coming out of university but to immigration. We have to import doctors because our students cannot enter university, since the key is in the hands of the college of physicians. Today,

January 28, 1976
Medical Care
there is a shortage of doctors. The minister said earlier that he was worried about a surplus of physicians, when actually there is a shortage. In the province of Quebec, we need
2,000	more doctors and yet our students are kept out of university. That is why we have to bring in immigrants, so that we may receive medical care from foreigners. I do not mind it, personally, I have nothing against them, but I would much rather see our French-Canadian students enter university freely. This is the one area in the province of Quebec where the situation is most dramatic.
A while ago the minister said: In the past, in 1968, there was one doctor for every 769 inhabitants, and today, there is one doctor for every 586 Canadians. I wonder where he gets those figures? In our areas with 6,000 people, we have two general practitioners. It is not surprising that a patient who needs to see a doctor must wait one or two weeks. But these doctors do their best. They are alone for 6,000 people. How can they do their job satisfactorily? The minister said earlier: There is some fear that there are too many doctors. I do not know whether he got that fear from the College of Physicians and Surgeons, but I think that they are afraid that there will be too many doctors because this would affect their salary. However, a greater number of doctors would be much more useful to the population. In my area, I can assure you that we could easily use four doctors instead of two and that they would earn a good living of $60,000 a year. But no, we are stuck. That is the problem. People say: That happens in the country, in rural areas; all the surgeons and specialists stay in the few large centres that we have in Quebec. I can see that the figures are distorted because they include all the specialists in the large centres. But if we consider only the doctors who serve the population, we can see that we need 2,000 more doctors in Quebec. Each year, I have seen with my own eyes students who dreamt of a medical career. They had grades of 90 and 92 per cent, but were rejected. Why? I do not dare speculate here. But let us see. It is the worst closed shop ever. In our areas where 92 per cent of the population is French-Canadian, we are treated by foreign doctors because our own people have not been able to enter this closed shop.
I believe that we must point this out. The College of Physicians and Surgeons seems to think that we are ignoramuses. That we cannot realize what is going on. The whole population has been aware of it for a long time and people know why they cannot see a doctor when necessary. This is why I was surprised to hear a while ago the minister say that there will probably be too many doctors in a few years. No.
I merely say to the minister: Do not be afraid, open the door, open the universities, and if you do not have enough universities, open the CEGEPs which are standing idle, which are half-empty, and start medical classes in there. That is a solution.
Let nobody tell me that we lack facilities. When in our areas CEGEPs and composite schools are half-empty and will be only one-third full within five years, let nobody tell me that we spend too many millions. Colleges with 30 or 35 classrooms are closed down and they are handed over for a nominal price to the municipalities. Don't you think this is too much? That is administration. That is why I said earlier that what is wrong is overadministration and bad

administration. We let the technocrats do as they please. And all they think about is to be overpaid for soft jobs, and then everything is fine. And as elected members of Parliament, we have nothing to say, we must obey the orders of technocrats. It requires less effort on its part if it lets all those technocrats do as they please and stays put. It only has to sign at the bottom of the letter but the real responsible people are still members of Parliament. And I think we fail in our duty by creating here through technocrats an irresponsible administration because members on the government side shirk their responsibilities, they pass them on to technocrats. It is true, some of your friends told me, they complained about that. There is a revolution in Quebec to have members of Parliament resume their jobs, their positions. Indeed, 250 Liberals in Quebec sat so the member of Parliament would resume his functions.
We travel through our ridings and know their needs street by street, parish by parish. And who comes up to manage all that, a technocrat who lives in Quebec City or Montreal who never understood what it was all about. And a legislation is prepared to try to improve health in Canada as in the province of Quebec, which is going to be discussed for a while. At present, everything is probably done, all the arrangements are probably made at the technocratic level, and that is going to be presented to the committee. Vote for, vote against, period. The majority is there. Amendments like that we can pass, and the more we do the worse the hospital service will be.
Now, to comfort us at the end, the minister tells us about the fund freeze in medical research. If there is something I am interested in it is medical research. I heard about the freeze, when all searchers live like beggars. Yet we need searchers. Indeed, I was speaking to two or three doctors who told me we would need three times more medical research here in Canada, and the funds for medical research just got frozen. What fear there is to give a little million dollars to try and find something new in medicine. And the funds are frozen for this year. Everything that is urgent gets frozen and all sorts of increases for insignificant things are allowed.
Finally, the minister tells us that he will undertake a fight. I noticed that when this bill is considered reforms or amendments will be examined with respect to the use of tobacco. I think it is time to do it, and the use of alcohol and drugs should also be added. I remember that, those past years, grants have been given to tobacco growers. How things change. A few years ago, Parliament voted grants for tobacco growers. Now, it is to be grants to control the use of tobacco. It has to be done, as it is in the case of alcohol, drugs and road safety. For weeks now, we have heard about seat belts; people think it is the answer to all problems. Of course, it is not.
The first problem to solve is, I think, the control of alcoholism, because one must not forget that 80 per cent of traffic accidents, and I have seen pretty bad one, are related to overdrinking. See what is happening: instead of talking about alcohol, or taking drastic measures, we talk about seat belts. I will tell you something, when a man is drunk, whether his seat belt is fastened or not, he will die in his car. Mind you, even if he is wearing his seat belt, he will die in his car. But this man who had too much to
January 28, 1976

drink-and this can happen to anybody-should have been warned against driving.
Let us see now what goes on. Go and watch people leaving night clubs and beer parlors late at night: 50 per cent of the drivers cannot walk straight and get behind the wheel, and no policeman is watching. There should be a policeman to tell them: "My friend, you are too drunk, you cannot drive in your condition, better leave your car and walk home." That should be the first thing to do. But you never see a policeman as people come out of night clubs and beer parlors. Why? Because that would be bad for the provincial liquor business. You have to realize that the provincial liquor business, the provincial Liquor Corporation, has to make money. So this chap is allowed to kill himself. You know that he is drunk, but you let him drive his car and, with this new reform, instead of being warned against driving, he will be fastened to his seat. He is going to be tied to his seat. As long as he has fastened his seat belt, he will have the right to go and kill himself. But if he has not, he will lose his insurance. If he gets killed without his seat belt, his insurance will not pay. That is the inconsistency in the reforms proposed.
We must absolutely stop talking about the seat belt. First of all, I do not believe in it, because I say that in 50 per cent of the cases, the seat belt may save your life, but in the other 50 per cent, it may be the cause of your death. It is strange, but we have not heard of such cases often. If a car is dumped into a river, and if its passengers all have their seat belts fastened, they will all die like rats. In 50 per cent of collisions, the air pressure causes passengers to be propelled out of the car. If they stay inside, however, the fire will start and they will be trapped inside. I say: let us begin at the beginning. Everybody admits that 80 per cent of car accidents are caused by alcohol. Let us make a legislation that will prevent that. As for high speed, it does not depend only on drivers, Madam Speaker. Car manufacturers are allowed to build racing cars that can do 150 miles an hour. Why is that, when the speed limit is 70, even on our super highways. These cars should be locked at 70 miles an hour. Why allow car manufacturers to make racing cars that can do 150 miles an hour, when such speed is illegal? So, nobody would expect to travel at such speed. It is better to cure the problem at the root instead of trying to alleviate it. But in the end, people try to explain away accidents. They say: he was killed for such and such reason probably because he did not have a safety belt which was probably not true. The thing is to take due precautions beforehand. Safety should start when a car is built. We should impose our conditions on the manufacturers. I submit this would be much more worthwhile than the minor reforms the minister proposed this afternoon.
Now, he referred to sports and sports promotion. I do not know exactly if the minister only wants to promote sports on the international level, as far as international competitions are concerned, but I urge him once again to think about our local and regional athletes. This is where he should start, at the beginning. How hard it is to get a few dollars for our local athletes! And even then, programs would still be needed so that our young people may improve their performance.
But no; grants will be given in every sphere related to international competition, but never will city or municipal
Medical Care
projects be accepted to help train local and regional athletes.
I do hope this matter of athletics will be discussed by the committee, so that help may be given to athletes from the bottom up, to encourage our own athletes, those who compete here, at home, in our province or elsewhere in Canada, before they go competing abroad.
I believe, Madam Speaker, I have already pointed this out to the hon. members in this House. I do hope this bill will not deal merely with the question of reducing costs, but also with the question of the services to the public, so that people will get better services, live in greater security in our area, and above all, live in a state of health that can be improved through the hospital centres that Canada like the province of Quebec can afford, considering the high cost of all such services. We pay enough taxes to have top quality hospital services, as the minister mentioned in his speech. But because of poor administration, a lack of supervision on the part of the departments, we live in the difficult conditions I have just described. I do hope this bill will improve the situation to some extent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gus Mitges (Grey-Simcoe):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate on Bill C-68. This afternoon the minister extolled the virtues of the health care program in Canada, describing it as among the best in the world. I do not dispute this. However, the same program is now in peril of losing its excellence and faces considerable downgrading to the detriment of the health of citizens from one end of Canada to the other. The tool the government is using to accomplish this is the bill now before us. If the measure is passed as introduced it will seriously undermine the quality of health care throughout our country.
I am not questioning the need to try to reduce costs and control spending especially now when restraint should be the number one priority if we ever hope to make any progress in containing the fires of inflation. What I am questioning is the absence of any prior consultation with the provinces in an effort to achieve economies in health care. It was done unilaterally by the federal government contrary to the recommendations of a 1969 task force report which recommended that consultation should take place between federal and provincial governments before any monetary changes in the program were considered.
To my mind, Madam Speaker, when one partner is not aware of what the other partner intends to do it cannot help but sow the seeds of confrontation. And confrontation is what the federal government is facing today as a result of its unilateral action. I feel sure this situation could have been avoided had the federal government chosen to embark on prior consultation with the provinces in an effort to resolve this problem in a businesslike and amicable way as between equal partners.
A further recommendation in the 1969 task force report on the cost of health services in Canada stated that ways must be found to restrain the growth of cost increases through better operation of the health structure now in existence. I have no quarrel with that recommendation. It is my opinion that whether in the running of a business, a

January 28, 1976
Medical Care
factory, or a home there will always be found, if one tries hard enough, ways to reduce costs and overhead expenses by eliminating waste, unnecessary frills and so on, without necessarily reducing the quality of service in the business field or the quality of life in the home. This is also true of a number of government programs presently in existence. Many of these should be eliminated entirely. Others in connection with which prudent spending of the taxpayer's dollars is only faintly evident or non-existent should be drastically curtailed.
On the other hand, there are programs which are commendable and from which the taxpayer receives his money's worth. Such a program is the medicare program, and that is why it is baffling to me to understand the government's decision to establish arbitrarily spending ceilings in relation to a scheme which has not demonstrated runaway cost increases to the extent other federally-sponsored projects have done.
Government spokesmen have maintained that health costs have risen by almost 20 per cent over the past year. I do not quarrel with this figure, but what the government fails to mention is that almost all the increase referred to is the direct result of escalating expenditures in hospitals, and not medical care generally. In the fiscal years 1972-73 and 1973-74 the increase in medical costs amounted only to 9.2 per cent and 7.2 per cent respectively; costs to the federal government have not been increasing at a greater rate than the national income.
Again, I ask why the central government has arbitrarily placed spending ceilings on a program which has not demonstrated the runaway cost increases of other federally sponsored programs? The answer lies in the fact that between 70 and 80 per cent of the total cost of medical care arises from salaries and wages. During a period of inflation such as we are now experiencing this means that an
increase in wages of 20 per cent will result in an increase in total budgetary outlay of 14 per cent to 16 per cent. By imposing ceilings the federal government is ensuring that it will not have to pay medical expenses arising from its inability to control inflation.
Bill C-68, if passed, will limit the federal cost-sharing contribution to medicare to an increase of 13 per cent in 1976-77, 10.5 per cent in 1977-78, and a figure thereafter to be determined in a way not yet established. There is no question in my mind that the imposition of these ceilings will markedly affect the health care delivery system. The federal government insists that if costs should rise above these figures it will be the responsibility of each province to pick up the tab for the difference. Consequently three situations could potentially arise: (1) provincial revenues would be drained, and other programs or priorities would have to be deferred indefinitely to meet the increased costs; (2) where applicable, that is, in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, and the Yukon Territory, premiums most likely would have to be increased in order to offset high provincial expenditures; (3) if the provinces cannot meet the extra costs, medical services will have to be reduced.
Therefore, while Bill C-68 basically follows the recommendation of the 1969 task force concerning the need to face the situation caused by rising health costs, should the government's exercise in clairvoyance fail to justify itself, Canadians will be faced with two alternatives-reduced health care services or increased taxes, may I call it six o'clock?
